claims.text: Applying an HEA coating to Q235 steel suppresses the onset of corrosion-related degradation.
Applying an HEA coating to Q235 steel suppresses the progression of corrosion-related degradation.
The HEA coating forms a dense barrier at the coating–steel interface.
The HEA coating is chemically inert under the proposed exposure conditions.
The dense HEA barrier limits oxygen penetration to the Q235 steel substrate.
The dense HEA barrier limits electrolyte penetration to the Q235 steel substrate.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a native oxide layer.
Minimizing defects in the HEA coating promotes its protective barrier function.
The density of defects in the HEA coating governs its microstructural integrity and corrosion protection.
Phase stability in the HEA coating contributes to coating and interface integrity.
The HEA coating acts as a passivating barrier that reduces exposure of the steel to corrosive agents.
Reducing exposure of Q235 steel to corrosive agents mitigates corrosion-product formation and propagation of degradation.
The chemical inertness of the HEA delays initiation of localized corrosion.
The stable microstructure of the HEA delays localized corrosion under temperature-induced stress variations.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, HEA-coated specimens will have a delayed corrosion-initiation time.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, HEA-coated specimens will have lower overall corrosion rates.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, HEA-coated specimens will form less corrosion product.
The protective effect applies to a uniform, defect-minimized HEA coating in chloride-rich environments from room temperature to approximately 50°C.
Significant coating defects may reduce or eliminate the protective effect.
Long-term performance during temperature and humidity cycling depends on coating microstructure and adhesion quality.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes applying the coating to 'pre-exposed Q235 steel,' whereas the material initial state specifies Q235 steel in its 'pre-exposure state.' These are different initial exposure histories.
